hero.text: Pearson's year-by-year English curriculum for international schools, from Year 1 to Year 9, and the two external tests that sit at the end of each stage.

blocks.title: This is a curriculum, not a single examination
text: Parents often say *my child does Edexcel* and mean one of several quite different things. The Edexcel **graded curriculum** described on these pages runs year by year from Year 1 to Year 9 and is taught in school; it is not the same as an International GCSE, which is a two-year qualification taken at the end of Year 11.
There are external tests, but only **two** in nine years: one at the end of Year 6 and one at the end of Year 9. Everything between them is taught and assessed inside the school.

blocks.title: The one difference that changes how you prepare
text: **iPrimary texts are pre-released.** The two Year 6 texts are published by Pearson at least four weeks before the test, and Pearson's own guidance recommends that schools spend around two weeks of lesson time - eight to ten hours - working on them. A Year 6 child who has not seen the texts before test day is at a serious and entirely avoidable disadvantage.
**iLowerSecondary texts are unseen.** The three Year 9 texts arrive in a Source Booklet with the paper. Preparation therefore has to be about method rather than about content.
Parents moving a child between schools should check which stage their child is in and whether the school has downloaded the pre-release.

blocks.title: How this guide handles Pearson's material
text: **Facts are stated; documents are linked, never copied.** Codes, timings, mark totals and assessment-objective weightings are facts about the qualification and are given here with their source. Pearson's curriculum documents, schemes of work, past papers and mark schemes belong to Pearson and are not reproduced on this site.

**The detailed year-by-year learning objectives are not published here.** Pearson releases the full curriculum only to subscribing centres, and it is theirs to release. What follows is the published structure, plus RCF English's own guidance and original practice material.

items.q: Is the Edexcel iPrimary curriculum the same as an International GCSE?
a: No. iPrimary covers Years 1 to 6 and iLowerSecondary covers Years 7 to 9. International GCSE is a separate two-year qualification taken in Years 10 and 11.

The three are designed to run into one another - iPrimary prepares for iLowerSecondary, which prepares for International GCSE English, either as a first language or as a second language - but they are different qualifications with different codes and different examinations.

items.q: Who is the Edexcel iPrimary English curriculum designed for?
a: Pearson states that it is designed for students who are **not** native speakers of English but who study most of their other subjects in English. It combines approaches from a first-language English curriculum with the progression and scaffolding that English-as-an-additional-language learners need.
This matters for parents choosing a school in a country such as Sri Lanka: the curriculum assumes English is the medium of instruction, not the home language.

items.q: How many external examinations are there between Year 1 and Year 9?
a: Two: the Year 6 Achievement Test (JEH11/01) and the Year 9 Achievement Test (LEH11/01).
Schools also use internal Progress Tests in other years, but those are set and marked within the school rather than externally certificated.

items.q: Can I download the full curriculum objectives?
a: Only through a subscribing school. Pearson publishes free overview documents describing the strands and giving sample objectives, and it publishes the specification, past papers and mark schemes openly. The complete year-by-year curriculum, schemes of work and lesson plans are released to centres that subscribe to the programme.
This site does not reproduce them. If you need them, ask your child's school, which will have them if it is registered.

items.q: Where can I find past papers for the Year 9 test?
a: On the [official iLowerSecondary English page](https://qualifications.pearson.com/en/qualifications/edexcel-international-lower-secondary-curriculum/english-2018.html), where Pearson publishes question papers and mark schemes for past series.
Use the mark schemes rather than only the papers. A Year 9 student who reads how the 30-mark writing task is actually marked will gain more than one who does another paper unmarked.

blocks.heading: The qualification at a glance
rows: Pearson Edexcel International Award in Primary English

blocks.heading: The curriculum: three strands
text: The iPrimary English curriculum is organised into six year groups, each building on the last. It contains **three main strands**, each divided into sub-strands. The strand names below are Pearson's; the commentary on each is RCF English's own.

parts.heading: 1. Spoken Language
text: Two sub-strands. This strand is not directly examined in the Year 6 test, which is written - but it underpins both of the others, and schools that treat it as optional tend to produce children who read accurately and write thinly.
bullets: **Receptive Language** - listening, following and understanding.
**Expressive Language** - speaking, explaining, discussing and presenting.

parts.heading: 2. Reading
text: Six sub-strands, one of which stops after Year 3. This is the largest strand and it carries half of the marks in the Year 6 test.
bullets: **Word Reading and Phonics** (up to Year 3) - decoding, letter-sound relationships, blending.
**Word Reading and Accuracy** - reading unfamiliar words correctly and fluently.
**Literal Comprehension** - finding information that is actually stated.
**Inferential Comprehension** - working out what is implied but not said. This is where most marks are won and lost.
**Text Structure and Purpose** - how a text is organised, and why.
**Grammar for Reading** - using grammatical knowledge to understand meaning.

parts.heading: 3. Writing
text: Six sub-strands. Note how much of this strand is technical accuracy rather than composition - which matches the test, where grammar, punctuation and spelling carry a quarter of the total mark on their own.
bullets: **Transcription and Phonics** - spelling and the sound-to-letter knowledge behind it.
**Vocabulary** - the range of words available and choosing between them.
**Composition** - planning, drafting and shaping a piece of writing.
**Handwriting and Word Processing** - legible handwriting and keyboard skills.
**Grammar for Writing** - sentence construction and control.
**Punctuation** - accuracy and its effect on meaning.

rows: Questions on the pre-released non-fiction text. Closed and short-open response.
Questions on the pre-released fiction text. Closed and short-open response.
Short-response questions, all based on the **fiction** text from Section A.
A single extended writing task, related to the theme of the Section A texts.
All questions in every section are compulsory.

blocks.heading: Assessment objectives and their exact weightings
blocks.caption: Percentages of the whole qualification, from the JEH11 specification. Reading accounts for 50%, grammar and punctuation for 25%, and writing for 25%.
rows: Retrieve information, events or ideas from texts
Deduce, infer or interpret information, events or ideas from texts
Identify and comment on the structure and organisation of texts
Explore the writers' use of language, at word and sentence level
Consider the writers' purposes and viewpoints, and the overall effect of the text on the reader
Demonstrate how accurate use of grammar, punctuation and spelling contribute to meaning
Write a response appropriate to task, audience and purpose
Organise writing by sequencing and structuring information appropriately and coherently
Communicate meaning in writing through the use of accurate grammar, punctuation and spelling

blocks.title: What those percentages tell you to teach
text: **Grammar and punctuation is the single largest objective at 25%** - larger than any reading objective and equal to the whole of writing. A quarter of this qualification rests on accuracy, and it is the most improvable thing on the list.

**Inference (RAO2, 15%) is the largest reading objective**, and it is three times the size of structure (RAO3, 5%). A child who can find stated facts but cannot say what a character is feeling will lose far more than one who cannot label a subheading.

**Accurate writing (WAO3, 10%) outweighs task and audience (WAO1, 8%) and organisation (WAO2, 7%).** In the 15-mark writing task, correctness matters more than ambition. A short, well-punctuated piece scores better than a long, exciting, error-strewn one.

blocks.heading: Using the pre-release properly
intro: The two Section A texts are published by Pearson at least **four weeks** before the test. Pearson's own guidance recommends that schools give the pre-release around **two weeks of lesson time, eight to ten hours**. The following sequence follows that guidance.

items.title: Get the texts and read them yourself first
text: Before any lesson. You cannot direct a child's attention to what matters in a text you met the same morning.

items.title: Read them aloud, with expression
text: Pearson recommends this explicitly. Children who have heard a text read well understand its tone, and tone is what RAO5 - 14% of the qualification - asks about.

items.title: Work on vocabulary in context and in isolation
text: Both. A child should know what a word means in the sentence where it appears **and** be able to say what it means on its own, because the test asks both ways.

items.title: Interrogate the writer's language and purpose
text: Why this word and not a plainer one? Who was this written for? What does the writer want the reader to feel? That is RAO4 and RAO5, 22% between them.

items.title: Look at the non-fiction text for audience, purpose and presentation
text: Headings, captions, images, layout - what each is doing and why it was put there.

items.title: Make sure every child has their own copy
text: To annotate, argue with and take home.

items.title: Be clear about what happens on the day
text: A clean **Source Booklet** containing both texts is supplied with the paper. **Marked-up copies of the pre-release are not permitted in the examination room.** Children who have relied on their annotations rather than on knowing the text can be badly caught out, so practise at least once with clean copies.

blocks.title: The practice material below is original RCF work
text: The activities that follow were written by RCF English. They are **not** Pearson materials, not past questions, and not sample assessment materials. They are written to rehearse the skills the assessment objectives name.

For official sample assessment materials and past papers, use the [iPrimary English page](https://qualifications.pearson.com/en/qualifications/edexcel-international-primary-curriculum/english-2018.html) on the Pearson website.

blocks.heading: Original RCF practice: the four skills the test rewards most
intro: Four short activities, each aimed at one of the heaviest assessment objectives. They can be used with any text, including the pre-release.

items.title: Inference ladder (RAO2, 15%)
text: Take any sentence from a story and ask three questions in order, always in this order:
**1. What does it say?** (literal - the child repeats it) **2. What does it tell us that it does not say?** (inference) **3. How do you know?** (evidence)
Example, on an original sentence: *Ravi checked the clock for the fourth time and moved his bag onto his lap.*

It says he checked the clock and moved his bag. It tells us he is anxious and expecting to leave soon. We know because *the fourth time* shows repetition, and moving a bag onto your lap is what people do just before standing up.
**Why it works:** step three is the one children skip, and it is the one the mark scheme rewards. A child who answers *he was nervous* with no evidence will not get the mark.

items.title: Two-column word work (RAO4, 8%)
text: Draw two columns. In the left, write the word the writer used. In the right, write the plainest word that would have done the same job.
*trudged* / *walked*. *whispered* / *said*. *ancient* / *old*.
Then ask one question only: **what is lost if we swap them?**
**Why it works:** it turns *the writer uses powerful vocabulary* - a sentence that earns nothing - into a statement about effect, which is what RAO4 asks for.

items.title: Punctuation repair (GAO1, 25%)
text: Give a child a short passage with the punctuation removed and ask them to put it back. Then - and this is the part that matters - ask them to explain **one** choice.
*the door was open which was strange because ravi had locked it that morning at least he thought he had*

**Why it works:** GAO1 is the largest single objective in the qualification, and it asks how punctuation *contributes to meaning*, not whether it is present. A child who can say *the comma is there because the second part explains the first* is answering the actual objective.

items.title: Fifteen-mark discipline (WAO1 to WAO3, 25%)
text: Set a writing task related to a text the child has read, and allow exactly **25 minutes** - the recommended time for Section C. Require three things and mark only those three:
**1.** Does it do what the task asked, for the right reader? (WAO1) **2.** Is it in a sensible order, with paragraphs? (WAO2) **3.** Is it accurate? (WAO3)

**Why it works:** children given an open writing task write until they are stopped. Section C is 15 marks in 25 minutes, and a controlled, correct, well-ordered piece of moderate length is exactly what those 15 marks are for.

blocks.heading: Preparing a Year 6 class
do: Download the pre-release the day it appears and plan two weeks around it.
Spend most of your reading time on inference, which is the largest reading objective.
Practise at least once with clean, unannotated copies of the texts.
Teach punctuation as something that changes meaning, not as a list of rules.
Time the writing task at 25 minutes so children learn what that feels like.
dont: Treat the pre-release as optional or leave it to the last week.
Let children rely on annotations they will not be allowed to bring in.
Spend equal time on all five reading objectives - they are worth 8, 15, 5, 8 and 14 per cent.
Reward long writing. Fifteen marks does not need three pages.
Use a dictionary in practice tests. They are not allowed in the real one.

blocks.heading: The curriculum: two strands
text: The iLowerSecondary English curriculum is organised into three year groups. It contains **two main strands**, each divided into sub-strands, with **Speaking and Listening woven through both** rather than standing as a strand of its own. The strand names below are Pearson's.

parts.heading: 1. Reading
text: Four sub-strands, carrying 40 of the 70 marks in the Year 9 test.
bullets: **Reading for Meaning** - understanding what a text says and implies.
**Responding to Texts** - forming and supporting a personal and then a critical response.
**Text Structure** - how a text is built and why it is built that way.
**Language Use** - the writer's choices at word and sentence level, and their effects.

parts.heading: 2. Writing
text: Three sub-strands, carrying 30 marks in a single extended task.
bullets: **Writing Processes** - planning, drafting, revising and proofreading.
**Whole Text** - shape, structure, paragraphing and coherence across a whole piece.
**Language Use** - vocabulary, sentence variety, grammar, punctuation and spelling.

blocks.title: How the curriculum grows across Years 7, 8 and 9
text: Pearson's published sample objectives show the same skills returning each year in a steadily more demanding form. The clearest example is the response objective, which moves through three stages:
**Year 7** - *identify* a writer's intention and viewpoint; express a **personal** response; make **simple** comparisons between two texts.

**Year 8** - *explore* a writer's intention and viewpoint; express a **critical** response by considering the text's features and their effects; make **developed** comparisons, including across different genres.
**Year 9** - *respond to* a writer's intention and viewpoint; **develop** a critical response; select a **range** of relevant, focused evidence.

The progression to notice is from *personal* to *critical*, and from *simple* to *developed* comparison. A Year 9 student still writing *I liked this text because it was interesting* is answering a Year 7 objective.

blocks.heading: The Year 9 Achievement Test: LEH11/01
blocks.caption: Verified from the official Summer 2022 paper. The recommended timings printed on the paper total 105 minutes exactly.
rows: Questions on three unseen texts linked by a theme - typically two non-fiction and one fiction - supplied in a Source Booklet. Question types include multiple choice answered with a cross in a box, short response and extended response.
One extended writing task, with bullet points to guide content.
All questions in both sections are compulsory.

blocks.title: Three pieces of advice printed on the paper itself
text: The official paper prints its own advice, and it is worth taking literally.

**"It is recommended that you read one text at a time and answer the questions on this text."** Students who read all three texts first, then start answering, lose time and confuse the texts. Read Text 1, answer the questions on Text 1, then move on.
**"Try to answer every question."** There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so a blank is a guaranteed nought.

**"There may be more space than you need."** The size of the answer box is not a hint about the length of the answer. Students routinely pad a two-mark answer to fill the space and lose time they need in Section B.

blocks.title: The practice material below is original RCF work
text: The activities that follow were written by RCF English. They are **not** Pearson materials, not past questions, and not sample assessment materials.

For official past papers and mark schemes, use the [iLowerSecondary English page](https://qualifications.pearson.com/en/qualifications/edexcel-international-lower-secondary-curriculum/english-2018.html) on the Pearson website.

blocks.heading: Original RCF practice: preparing for three unseen texts
intro: The Year 9 texts are unseen, so preparation cannot be about content. It has to be about a method that works on any text put in front of you.

items.title: The four-minute first read
text: Give a student any unfamiliar article and exactly four minutes. At the end they must write, without looking back, four things: **who wrote it, who for, what they want the reader to think, and one word that gave it away.**

**Why it works:** Section A gives about 23 minutes per text including the questions, so the first read has to be fast and purposeful. This drills the habit of reading for viewpoint from the first sentence, which is what the *Responding to Texts* and *Language Use* sub-strands both depend on.

items.title: Personal to critical
text: Take any response a student has written and make them rewrite it once, under one rule: **remove every use of *I* and replace it with a statement about the text.**
*I found the ending sad* becomes *The ending is made sad by the short final sentence, which stops the story before the reader is ready.*

**Why it works:** this is exactly the Year 7 to Year 9 progression Pearson describes - personal response to critical response. It is the single largest jump in the whole curriculum and most students make it by accident, late, or not at all.

items.title: Comparison in one sentence
text: Give a student two short texts on the same subject and allow them **one sentence** to compare the writers' viewpoints. The sentence must contain both writers and one point of difference.
*Where the first writer treats the change as a loss, the second treats it as overdue.*

**Why it works:** *developed comparison* is a Year 8 and 9 objective, and students fail it by writing a paragraph about one text followed by a paragraph about the other. Forcing both into one sentence makes genuine comparison unavoidable. Once they can do it in one sentence they can expand it; the reverse never works.

items.title: Thirty-five minutes, three checks
text: Set an extended writing task with bullet points, allow exactly **35 minutes**, and require five of those minutes to be spent at the end on three checks only: **sentence endings, paragraph breaks, and one repeated word replaced.**

**Why it works:** 30 marks is a large share of the paper for a single task, and *Language Use* sits inside the Writing strand alongside structure. Five minutes of checking recovers more marks than five minutes of extra content, and students will not do it unless it is timetabled.

blocks.heading: Year 9 readiness checklist
items: Can the student read an unfamiliar text and state its viewpoint in under five minutes?
Do their responses discuss the text rather than their own feelings about it?
Can they compare two writers in a single sentence?
Do they select short, focused evidence rather than copying out long quotations?
Have they written a 30-mark task in 35 minutes, with clean copies and no dictionary?
Do they leave answers blank? (They should not - there is no penalty for a wrong answer.)
